note: Song-craft rules for beat-driven dance music (pop, dance pop, house, hip-hop, funk) scored to muted dance video. Drawn from concept-level audio analysis of 11 pop hits (tempo, sections, low end, drum families, loop lengths; no notes, melodies or lyrics) plus widely taught production practice; evidence says which. Ordered so the most important rules per call come first.
tracks: Justin Bieber - What Do You Mean?
Why Don't We - Trust Fund Baby
Mark Ronson ft. Bruno Mars - Uptown Funk

rules.text: Lock one tempo for the whole piece and quantise every part to it: no rubato, no ritardando, no accelerando, not even at the end.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: tempo constant within 0.05 BPM end to end (82-132 BPM), two methods agree

rules.text: Pick the kick family from the tempo: about 115-130 BPM put the kick on every beat; 80-110 BPM use a syncopated kick under a backbeat; above 130 keep four-on-the-floor or switch to half-time.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: kick on all four beats in the 4 tracks at 115-125 BPM; syncopated kicks at 82-107; one clap per bar at 132; the 131 track turns four-on-the-floor in late choruses

rules.text: Shape energy mainly by taking kick and bass out and bringing them back; volume alone barely changes between a verse with the beat and a chorus.
rules.evidence: measured on 9 of 11 tracks: a 4+ bar block with low-end share under 10% of the chorus; chorus only 0.3-5.6 dB (median 2.8) louder than beat-verse

rules.text: Make the hook one or two bars long, four to eight notes on a memorable rhythm cell, ending so it loops straight back into its own start.
Repeat the two- or four-bar loop exactly through a section; at each four- or eight-bar line change one thing only: a layer, the last bar, an answer.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: harmony repeats with a 2- or 4-bar period inside sections; similarity at 8-bar lag almost equals 4-bar lag

rules.text: Reject a phrase that leaves the loop or hook for new melodic material; accept one that repeats it with a single clear change or none.
Mark a scene cut without stopping the beat: land the change on the nearest bar line with a crash, a fill into it, or a one-bar drum drop.
rules.evidence: general practice; tempo never broke in 11 of 11 measured tracks

rules.text: End on a downbeat at full tempo: after the last chorus either strip layers over four to eight bars or hit one final chord and kick and stop dead.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: no tempo change at the end of any track

rules.text: When following the dancers live, change sections only at the next four- or eight-bar line, and change layers, never the tempo.
Plan sections as whole 4-bar multiples, usually 8 or 16 bars; links and breakdowns may be 4. Put every section change on a 4-bar line.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: section runs 4-24 bars; 42 of 66 largest changes on the first or last bar of a 4-bar block

rules.text: Use a riffy two-bar loop for funk, hip-hop and slower pop; use a four-chord, four-bar loop for dance-pop and house.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: 2-bar loops in all 5 tracks at 82-115 BPM; 4-bar loops in 5 of 6 tracks at 116-132 BPM

rules.text: Change chords at most once per bar, often once every two bars; a one-chord vamp for a whole verse or drop is normal.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: bass root changes 0.5-0.95 times per bar; one bass note held 4+ bars in 2 tracks

rules.text: Before the biggest section, strip the low end for four to eight bars or cut it for the last one or two beats, so kick and bass return on the downbeat.
rules.evidence: measured on 10 of 11 tracks: 23 of 42 high-energy arrivals followed a bass-less block or a last-beats dip (ordinary bar lines ~15%)

rules.text: Give the hook at least one syncopation, a note anticipating the beat by an eighth or sixteenth; a hook of even quarter notes sounds like a hymn.
Lock the bass to the kick: bass notes start with kick hits or just after them and rest where the snare lands; do not let a held bass smear the kick.
Prefer the draft whose rhythm locks to kick and snare and leaves rests; reject drafts of continuous even notes with no space.
For a minor scene cut change just one layer at the bar line: hats in or out, a filter step, or a new percussion loop.
Bring kick and bass in within the first four to eight bars and the first full chorus or drop by about bar 16-24; avoid a long quiet introduction.
rules.evidence: measured on 10 of 11 tracks: kick+bass in by bar 0-11 (median about bar 7, 15 s); first loudest block median bar 18

rules.text: Bring the chorus or drop back three or four times with the same hook; make each return different through arrangement, not new material.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: the top-energy block recurs 2-5 times (median 4)

rules.text: Keep eighth notes straight; if anything, swing only the sixteenths, and lightly. A shuffled or triplet feel is a different style.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: offbeat eighths at 0.50-0.54 of the beat; sixteenths straight in 2 tracks, slightly late in 1

rules.text: In stripped sections take away weight, not motion: drop kick and bass but keep hats, claps or rhythmic chords running so the pulse never stops.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: onset density in stripped blocks 77-135% of the chorus

rules.text: Raise intensity with density and layers: sixteenth hats, extra percussion, a doubled hook an octave up. Do not rely on getting louder.
rules.evidence: measured on 10 of 11 tracks: choruses had more onsets per beat than verses in 9 of 10 (+0.04 to +0.8)

rules.text: Put the biggest, longest full-energy block in the second half, usually the last chorus after a breakdown; do not peak in the first minute.
rules.evidence: measured on 7 of 11 tracks: the longest full-energy run sits in the second half

rules.text: Plan one breakdown of four to eight bars about two-thirds through: kick and bass out, pad or the hook alone, then a fill into the final chorus.
rules.evidence: measured on 6 of 11 tracks: a 4-bar thinned block at roughly 50-75% of the track

rules.text: Shape phrases as call and response: the hook in bars one and three, an answer from another sound, a fill or silence in bars two and four.
Keep the hook in a narrow range, about a fifth to an octave, using repeated notes and small steps with at most one leap for identity.
Judge a hook by whether it could loop 16 times without tiring and be recognised from its rhythm alone; prefer catchy over developed.
Vary mostly the last bar of each four- or eight-bar phrase with a fill, stop or pickup; the first three bars repeat the loop.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: big bar-to-bar changes cluster on the last and first bar of 4-bar blocks

rules.text: Use short stops: mute everything, or just the drums, for one or two beats at the end of a bar, then re-enter on the downbeat.
rules.evidence: measured on 6 of 11 tracks: stops of 0.5-2.3 beats, mostly starting on beat 3 or 4 (downbeat inferred, moderate confidence)

rules.text: End every fourth or eighth bar with a fill in its last one or two beats: snare or tom run, hat roll, reverse cymbal or drum drop.
Open with a partial texture for four to eight bars, the hook riff, chords or filtered drums alone; start straight on the beat if the dance starts at once.
rules.evidence: measured on 10 of 11 tracks: a thinned intro of 1-11 bars before kick and bass

rules.text: Make verse and chorus differ by arrangement (kick pattern, bass in or out, hats, an extra layer), not by new chords or a new tempo.
rules.evidence: general practice; loops held across sections in the measured tracks

rules.text: Choose the palette by job: kick, snare or clap, hats, one bass, one chord layer, one lead hook sound, plus effects. Leave out orchestral sections.
Give the range below about 150 Hz to kick and bass only; in full sections they should dominate the mix weight. Keep chords and leads above.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: 30-150 Hz held 41-83% of mix energy in full sections

rules.text: With no singer, carry the hook on a lead synth, pluck, brass stab or chopped-vocal-like sound, and feature it in the drop or post-chorus.
Add layers in this order as energy rises: chords, hats, kick, bass, clap or snare, lead hook, extra percussion and top effects; remove them in reverse.
Put the snare or clap on beats two and four in most sections; once per bar on beat three for half-time; a 3+3+2 placement for Latin or dancehall feels.
rules.evidence: measured on 10 of 11 tracks: backbeat in 8 tracks, once per bar in the 132 BPM track, 3+3+2 in the 100 BPM track

rules.text: Change the drum pattern only at section lines: lighter kick or half-time in verses, full pattern in the chorus, kick out in the breakdown.
rules.evidence: measured on 2 of 11 tracks: kicks per bar rose from about 2-3 in verses to 4 in later choruses

rules.text: Build into a drop with a low-pass filter closing over four to eight bars plus a noise riser or snare roll, then open fully on the downbeat.
Duck pads and bass under the kick with sidechain pumping in four-on-the-floor sections so each kick punches through.
Use hats to set density: eighths in verses, sixteenths or open off-beat hats in choruses, rolls only as end-of-bar punctuation.
Mark each new block's downbeat with a crash or impact and the return of whatever was taken out before it.
Write bass with rests, octave jumps and short slides into the next root; keep long held bass notes for breakdowns or 808 sections.
In trap or half-time sections hold a sub or 808 on one or two notes for four or more bars and let the kick pattern carry the rhythm.
rules.evidence: measured on 2 of 11 tracks: one bass note held for 4+ bars across most of a section

rules.text: End each four-bar phrase by setting up the next downbeat with a fill, a held note, a drop-out or the loop's turnaround, never a final-sounding cadence.
For a big scene change, stop everything for one or two beats just before the bar line, then bring the full beat back on the downbeat.
rules.evidence: general practice; stops measured on 6 of 11 tracks

rules.text: If a cut falls mid-bar, hit it with a short stab or impact on the nearest beat and save the section change for the next four-bar line.
Use a riser over the last one or two bars when a cut leads to a bigger scene, and a downlifter or reverse sweep when it leads to a calmer one.
Do not penalise exact repetition: a phrase identical to the previous one is correct unless the plan asks for a change at that block line.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: within-section loops repeat with high similarity

rules.text: Do not develop a long melody phrase by phrase; restate the short hook and change the arrangement around it instead.
Do not change chords every beat, build cadences or modulate through keys; loops, vamps and pedal bass are normal here.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: 2- or 4-bar loops, about one bass change per bar or less

rules.text: Do not shape sections with long crescendos and diminuendos; energy steps up or down at block lines by adding or removing layers.
Never leave a passage with no pulse: outside a short stop, something rhythmic (hats, clap, chopped chords) must mark the beat.
rules.evidence: measured on 11 of 11 tracks: stripped blocks kept 1.7-4.6 onsets per beat

rules.text: Do not move the hook up by steps phrase after phrase; keep its pitch level and vary rhythm, register by octave, or the sound carrying it.
Write the hook so it fits every pass of the chord loop unchanged; a line that only works over one chord change is a melody, not a hook.
Leave rests inside the hook: a beat or two of silence per bar gives the dancers an accent and leaves room for an answer.
Reject a phrase that puts melody in the bass register or long low notes over the kick and bass range.
Keep chords in the middle register as short stabs or a sidechained pad; avoid thick low voicings and doubled lines.
Make the sound produced, not hall-like: tight drums, short dry synths, reverb kept short except for single hanging notes in breakdowns.
Stay in one key for the whole piece; choose minor or a minor-leaning mode for dark, driving moves and major for bright, celebratory ones.
Map the dancers' energy to the layer plan: bigger movement gets kick, bass or hats added at the next block line; calmer movement gets them removed.
For an outro, remove layers in reverse order every four bars, or loop the hook alone, ending on a bar line rather than fading out mid-phrase.
If the dancers hit a sudden accent, answer it with a stab, a drop-out or a fill inside the current groove rather than a new section.
